data.title: Zemplín – a Celtic (Dacian?) sacrificial site
data.excerpt: At the foot of the Szélmalomdomb slope near the well-known hillfort at Zemplín, a sacrificial site of the La Tène period came to light in the 1960s. A 40 cm thick layer of deliberately deposited clay vessels also held 68 metal finds, among them iron fetters whose only known parallel comes from England.
data.metaTitle: Zemplín – a Celtic sacrificial site of the La Tène period
data.metaDescription: Beside the hillfort at Zemplín a La Tène sacrificial site was found in the 1960s, with a thick layer of deliberately deposited clay vessels and weapons.

children.text: At Zemplín, close to the well-known hillfort in the locality known as Kertalja (Pod záhradami – Below the Gardens), at the foot of the Szélmalomdomb slope (Windmill Hill), where a barrow cemetery of the Roman period lies, a sacrificial site of the La Tène period was discovered in the 1960s. The feature contained a 40 cm thick layer of deliberately deposited objects, mainly clay vessels and fragments of them, but also 68 metal finds including two coins. Pot-shaped vessels clearly predominate among the vessels. Some of them still recall forms of the Early Iron Age, but most of them are typically Dacian. A less numerous group is formed by Celtic products, namely grey, painted or graphite-coated wares with typical vertical grooving.

All the kinds of pottery found at the sacrificial site are also known from the hillfort and the settlement below it, that is, from places where occupation of the Late Iron Age is attested. The range of metal objects is more varied. Weapons were found in the greatest numbers, above all javelin heads and spearheads. Of the riding equipment, the chief items are spurs. Nor are working tools missing: knives, small axes, a sickle, awls, punches and wedges, as well as so-called structural ironwork: nails and cramps. It is hard to determine the original purpose of the iron rings of various sizes that were found at the sacrificial site. As yet we know of no parallel to the fragment of a horseshoe in find assemblages of the 1st century BC. Since, however, it was found at Zemplín in an undisturbed part of the Celtic–Dacian layer, it may be assumed that it belongs to it.

children.text: The most remarkable find at the sacrificial site was a set of iron fetters. They consist of two semicircles joined by a hinge and of a chain with which they were closed. They are fairly large, since, unlike present-day ones, they were put not on the hands but on the neck of the captive. The chain could have served for tethering, or the captive was held by it while being moved. The only similar fetters datable to the 1st century BC known so far come from England. Although the distance between England and Zemplín is considerable, both pieces come from a Celtic milieu, and so it may be imagined that similar customs in the treatment of captives prevailed in both places.

Among the objects deposited at the sacrificial site there is surprisingly little jewellery and ornament. Only a single iron brooch was found, of the kind that is among the commonest of that period. Two small bronze rings could have been part of bronze belts, or they could also have been worn as finger rings. The only more splendid piece consists of the metal parts of an astragal belt. The belt itself was originally of leather, with bronze clasps and decorative plates at both ends. On each side there were twenty plastically modelled links, which gradually decreased in size. The links, like the clasp itself, bear fine punched decoration. Astragal belts are known from the 1st century in the Carpathian Basin, but we find them more often in the territory south of the Alps. It may be assumed that the find from Zemplín reached the area as a trade item from the south-west.

children.text: The quantity, the deposition and above all the composition of the finds from the feature uncovered in the locality known as Kertalja allow us to assume that part of a cult place – a sacrificial site – was uncovered here. Similar sacrificial sites are known from contemporary sites above all in Switzerland and Germany, but also in Slovakia, for example at Havránok in Liptovská Mara and at Prosné. These are places to which the people of that time brought offerings to the deities, not infrequently human ones, which protected them from their enemies. At Zemplín no human remains were found at the sacrificial site. Here they gathered only what they regarded as most precious: vessels with food, working tools that secured their livelihood, weapons that protected them from enemies. These gifts were to serve to appease the deities, or to win their favour in securing a good harvest, driving away diseases and the like.
